exercise.name: 45 degrees Bycicle Twisting Crunch

reference.title: 45 degrees Bycicle Twisting Crunch
reference.listing: Page could not be read (gymvisual.com is blocked by the network proxy); movement taken from the exercise name and standard coaching practice

exercise.mechanics: Compound (trunk flexion with rotation, alternating hip and knee flexion)

breathing.pattern: Breathe out as each elbow turns toward the opposite knee; breathe in as you pass through the middle. Breathe steadily, no breath-holding.

prescription.tempo: Slow pedalling, about 1-1.5 s per side; a short pause at each twist
prescription.progression: Slower pedalling, longer pause at each twist, straight leg lower to the floor

cues.text: Sit on the mat, lean back to about 45 degrees and lift both feet. Fingertips behind the head, elbows wide, chest up.
Breathe out, turn the right elbow toward the left knee as the right leg extends long and low.
Switch: left elbow toward the right knee, left leg long.
Keep the trunk at 45 degrees; turn from the ribs, not the elbows.
Pedal smoothly; the feet never touch the floor.
Return to the middle, both knees bent, and breathe.

mistakes.mistake: Rounding and collapsing back toward the floor
mistakes.fix: Keep the chest up and the trunk at about 45 degrees; shorten the set if it sinks.

mistakes.mistake: Pulling the head with the hands
Flapping the elbows instead of turning the trunk
mistakes.fix: Turn the shoulder toward the knee.
Slow, controlled twists with a short pause.

kinematics.norm: Held at about 45 degrees from the floor, balanced on the buttocks (exercise name; clinical opinion)
Shoulder turns toward the opposite knee; elbow aims at the knee (ACE 2001 for the floor version); rotation amount is clinical opinion
Knee drawn toward the chest to meet the opposite elbow (clinical opinion)
Extends long and low without touching the floor (clinical opinion)
Slow pedalling (ACE 2001 for the floor version)

sources.title: GymVisual #1347, 45 degrees Bycicle Twisting Crunch, video (movement reference; page not readable here)
ACE-sponsored study, Francis and Davis (San Diego State University Biomechanics Lab) 2001, best and worst abdominal exercises, 30 adults, EMG relative to a crunch (ACE FitnessMatters, May/June 2001)
Oliva-Lozano and Muyor 2020, core muscle activity during physical fitness exercises: a systematic review (Int J Environ Res Public Health 17(12):4306)
Marshall and McGill 2010, the role of axial torque in disc herniation (Clin Biomech 25:6-9), porcine model

cautions: Stop if you feel sharp, radiating or nerve-type pain.
Muscle glow colours and activation curves are illustrative, not measured EMG.
The ACE result is from a magazine-published lab study (EMG relative to a crunch), not a peer-reviewed paper; treat the ranking as indicative.

Repeated loaded flexion combined with twisting promoted disc delamination in a porcine model (Marshall and McGill 2010); people with disc problems or flexion intolerance should pick a dead bug or side plank instead.
The leaned-back hold loads the hip flexors and low back; stop if the low back aches and use the floor air bike instead.
modify: Neck strain: rest the head in the hands without pulling, or cross the arms on the chest.
Low back arches: keep the straight leg higher.
Pregnancy or diastasis recti: avoid curl-up twists.
regressions: Feet on the floor, alternate elbow to opposite knee one side at a time.
progressions: Slower pedalling with a 2 s pause at each twist.
Straight leg lower toward the floor.

muscleNotes.core: Rectus abdominis holds the trunk at 45 degrees against gravity the whole set (an isometric hold, unlike the floor version where it curls). The floor bicycle maneuver gave the highest rectus activity of 13 exercises in the ACE 2001 study; this seated version was not measured (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.obliques_r: Obliques turn the trunk so the elbow travels toward the opposite knee: the external oblique on the side of the moving elbow and the internal oblique on the knee side. Oblique activity was about 2.9 times a crunch, second only to the captain's chair (ACE 2001).
muscleNotes.obliques_l: Obliques turn the trunk so the elbow travels toward the opposite knee: the external oblique on the side of the moving elbow and the internal oblique on the knee side. Oblique activity was about 2.9 times a crunch, second only to the captain's chair (ACE 2001).
muscleNotes.hip_flexors_r: Iliopsoas works hard here: it holds the legs up and also helps hold the trunk leaning back (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.hip_flexors_l: Iliopsoas works hard here: it holds the legs up and also helps hold the trunk leaning back (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.quads_r: Straighten the extending leg and help hold it up (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.quads_l: Straighten the extending leg and help hold it up (clinical opinion).
